statuses.label: Qualified or judged
statuses.description: Numerically qualified (a registered protocol passed) or judged (used in a registered experiment), in its declared scope.

statuses.label: Implemented and guarded
statuses.description: On main with its tests and guards: the plan's 'implemented' and 'guarded' levels. Not yet qualified by a registered protocol.

statuses.label: Established
statuses.description: Built earlier and in routine use: older model families and shared infrastructure. Scope and evidence are in each guide.

statuses.label: Designed
statuses.description: A design or protocol is written or accepted; the code is not on main.

statuses.label: Planned
statuses.description: Named in the plan or roadmap; not started.

statuses.label: Failed qualification
statuses.description: Built, then failed its registered qualification. Kept as evidence and not relied on.

statuses.label: External reference
statuses.description: Outside the engine: a reference simulator or data set, run out of process and compared through saved outputs.

representations.label: Simulated
representations.description: The engine evolves this state step by step, with material, charge and energy accounted for.

representations.label: Modelled in aggregate
representations.description: Represented as a population, count or rate law, not as individual molecules. Shapes drawn for it are illustrations.

representations.label: Prescribed
representations.description: Happens on a schedule the experiment sets; the cell does not decide it.

representations.label: Illustration only
representations.description: Drawn for orientation. Nothing in the engine stands behind it yet.

model_groups.label: Composite tissue model
model_groups.description: resolved_pump_composite@1: the pump tissue model's own step plus declared operators. These parts run together in one model today. Its inner tissue model is being rebuilt in place as one modular model; that work is not on main.

model_groups.label: Earlier tissue families
model_groups.description: The older resolved-tissue families, one module per feature combination. Calcium, fuel, mitochondria, regulation and repair run together here. Their physics moves into the composite model in stages, as uses need it (D167).

model_groups.label: Separate engines
model_groups.description: Models that run on their own: vertex mechanics and the regulatory circuits.

relation_kinds.label: uses
relation_kinds.description: The first part imports the second in the source code.

relation_kinds.label: is an operator of
relation_kinds.description: Registered as an operator of the composite model.

relation_kinds.label: requires
relation_kinds.description: The operator declares that this law must come before it.

relation_kinds.label: writes
relation_kinds.description: The operator declares that it changes this state and books the change.

relation_kinds.label: provides
relation_kinds.description: The operator provides this state to the rest of the model as its current value.

relation_kinds.label: reads
relation_kinds.description: The operator reads a value another operator provides.

relation_kinds.label: cannot combine with
relation_kinds.description: The composite refuses this pair: one operator reads a value as declared while the other changes it, or both provide the same value.

relation_kinds.label: wraps
relation_kinds.description: The composite runs this model's own step.

relation_kinds.label: runs
relation_kinds.description: The experiment runs this engine model or operator.

relation_kinds.label: would extend
relation_kinds.description: A planned or designed part, and what it builds on.

relation_kinds.label: delivers
relation_kinds.description: A plan gate, or a round of work, and a part it is meant to deliver.

relation_kinds.label: is implemented by
relation_kinds.description: A capability and the engine parts behind it.

relation_kinds.label: has its law in
relation_kinds.description: The engine law that acts on this unit is in this part of the engine (from the law inventory, checked against the code).

relation_kinds.label: is drawn in the cell view as
relation_kinds.description: The part of the cell view that stands for this unit.

proteins.title: Protein atlas
proteins.summary: From Cells' own law inventory, with links out to the public protein atlases. The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell.
proteins.caveat: Shapes are schematic, drawn from subunit counts, and not to scale. A grey form is a generic law: no protein is assigned.

review.text: Reviews on 14 and 15 November 2026 found no channel, pump, transporter or junction law among them. Two cases are the lead's to classify: secretion and uptake across a membrane, and the binding of molecules to sites.

mappings.label: Assigned in source
mappings.description: The law, its documents or the source it cites names the protein. This records a label; the kind of evidence on each law says what stands behind it.

mappings.label: Candidate
mappings.description: The law models a named native current or channel class. Which gene products carry it is the inventory's inference.

mappings.label: Generic
mappings.description: The law is deliberately generic, phenomenological or manufactured. Products are listed as candidates only.

evidence.label: Expressed isoform
evidence.description: The cited data come from the named isoform, expressed on its own.

evidence.label: Isoform named in the title
evidence.description: The cited source names the isoform in its title; the inventory read no further detail.

evidence.label: Native current
evidence.description: The cited data are a current recorded from native cells, not from an isolated isoform.

evidence.label: Neuron model
evidence.description: The cited source is a model of a neuron.

evidence.label: Derived reduction
evidence.description: A reduced (Morris-Lecar) form of the named channel.

evidence.label: No detail in the source
evidence.description: The source gives no detail on what the coefficients were measured from.

atlases.label: E. coli
atlases.plain: A rod-shaped bacterium of the animal gut with 4,403 proteins in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12. The units of the law inventory are machines of animal cells; this is what the same families' signatures find in it.
method: The organism's proteins are the 4,403 reviewed entries of UniProt's reference proteome UP000000625 (release 2026_04), one protein each.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources.

A unit counts as found only where a protein carries the signature of a family that makes the machine itself (the subunit that forms the channel, or the pump's own chain). A protein that carries only the signature of a family that goes with the machine (a regulator, an accessory subunit) is no candidate: the unit's note names it, and it is listed under extra. This reading is the file's own.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the planarian, Syn3A and M. pneumoniae atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Each signature was looked for among the InterPro entries UniProt gives each of the 4,403 proteins. No unit's own family was found; 1 protein carries the signature of an accessory family alone.
A control for every signature: how many reviewed UniProtKB entries of all bacteria carry it; each unit's note gives what came back.

8 further signatures, of the channels a bacterium could have (potassium, chloride, magnesium, water and membrane-stretch channels), were looked for as well; the 15 proteins that carry them are listed under extra (the potassium channel domain (kch); the large-conductance mechanosensitive channel (MscL) (mscL); the mechanosensitive channel MscS (mscK, mscM, mscS, ybdG, ybiO and ynaI); chloride channels of the ClC family (clcA, clcB and yfeO); aquaporins and their relatives (major intrinsic proteins) (aqpZ and glpF); CorA-type magnesium channels (corA and zntB)), with the cell's P-type ATPases and the catalytic head of its ATP synthase.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

atlases.label: Fruit fly
atlases.plain: The fruit fly of the laboratory, with 13,814 genes in UniProt's reference proteome. This is what the family signatures of Cells' machines find among the one protein shown for each gene.
method: The fly's proteins are the 13,814 of UniProt's gene-by-gene set of the reference proteome UP000000803 (release 2026_04): one for each gene, 3,850 with a reviewed entry and 9,964 with an unreviewed one.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the other species' atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.

Each signature was looked for among the InterPro entries UniProt gives each protein. A unit counts as found only where a protein carries the signature of a family that makes the machine itself; an accessory family alone does not make it found.
Where no protein carries the family the engine's law names and proteins carry another family asked for the same machine (innexins, for gap junctions), the finding is 'different family'.

A product with a reviewed entry is listed as a reviewed entry, one with an unreviewed entry as a family signature. Either is a candidate by family: several units of one family (the Kv1 channels) list the same proteins, and nothing here says which protein does which unit's work.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.

atlases.label: M. pneumoniae
atlases.plain: A small bacterium of the human airways with 688 proteins in its genome record, audited beside JCVI-syn3A for measured data to validate Cells against; the units of the law inventory are machines of animal cells, and it has none of them.
method: The organism's proteins are the 688 protein products of one frozen genome annotation, GenBank U00089.2: the genome of strain M129 as its submitters re-annotated it in 2000. UniProtKB holds a reviewed entry for 687 of them, and UniProt's archive (UniParc) holds all 688 sequences letter for letter, with the family signatures on each.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources, and what was read but not copied is in not_copied.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the planarian and Syn3A atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Each signature was looked for on all 688 sequences. None was found, for any unit.
A control for every zero: the same signature was asked of the UniProtKB entries of all mollicutes, the class of bacteria the organism belongs to; each unit's note gives what came back.

Eight further signatures, of the channels a bacterium could have (potassium, chloride, magnesium, water and membrane-stretch channels), were looked for as well. Seven were not found, although each is carried by UniProtKB entries of other mollicutes. One was: the family of water and glycerol channels, on the glycerol facilitator GlpF.

Under extra are nine of the organism's own membrane machines that bear on what the atlas draws and match no unit. Each has a reviewed UniProtKB entry of this strain and is listed by it; their functions are assigned by curators from sequence, not measured in this organism.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

atlases.label: Planarian
atlases.plain: A freshwater flatworm that regrows its whole body from a fragment; it is the planarian the databases know best, with 1,588 UniProtKB entries, more than all other planarians together, and a chromosome-scale genome with predicted genes.
method: Species: UniProt holds 1,588 entries for Schmidtea mediterranea (4 reviewed), more than half of the 2,784 it holds for all planarians (the order Tricladida; among the others, Dugesia japonica 499, Girardia tigrina 81, Schmidtea polychroa 74, Dugesia ryukyuensis 23), and a proteome for no planarian. WormBase ParaSite holds a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Schmidtea mediterranea with gene models; the assembly is described by Ivanković and others 2024. So the atlas is of Schmidtea mediterranea.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources, and what was read but not copied is in not_copied.

Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates: the InterPro signatures they carry were read from UniProt, and one or two that mark the family were chosen. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Curated entries first: UniProt has 4 reviewed entries for the species, and none belongs to a family the atlas draws.
Named in a publication: a planarian protein counts as named only where the saved abstract, or the saved open-access text, of the paper uses the name. 4 products rest on this.

Family signature: unreviewed UniProtKB entries of the species that carry the signature, and gene models that carry it. The gene models are those of one genome annotation (WBPS19 of WormBase ParaSite, assembly schMedS3_haplotype1): 17,294 genes with a predicted protein. The ones the atlas names are listed in data/proteins/planarian/reference_proteins.tsv. A model carries a signature if that annotation's own InterPro matches say so, or if its predicted protein is, letter for letter, a sequence that carries it in UniProt's archive (InterPro 111.0).
A UniProtKB sequence and a gene model are given as one product when at least 80% of the sequence's 8-residue words occur in the model's predicted protein and no other gene reaches half of that share.

Where a signature found nothing, it was also asked of all 98,660 planarian sequences in UniProt's archive, of the UniProtKB entries of all flatworms and of reviewed human entries; the unit's note gives what came back.

A product found by signature is a candidate, never an established counterpart. Counts are gene models in one haplotype of one genome assembly, not genes confirmed in the animal, and short models may be fragments.
No similarity search against other species was run, and no product is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

atlases.label: Syn3A
atlases.plain: A bacterium with a designed, minimised genome of 452 protein-coding genes, proposed as the first whole-cell validation organism for Cells; the units of the law inventory are machines of animal cells, and it has none of them.
method: The organism's proteins are the 455 protein products of one frozen genome annotation, GenBank CP016816.2 (annotation of 12 April 2018): 452 kept from Mycoplasma mycoides and 3 added for genetic manipulation. UniProtKB holds no entry of the organism; UniProt's archive (UniParc) holds exactly these 455 sequences, with the family signatures on each.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources, and what was read but not copied is in not_copied.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the planarian atlas asks. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Each signature was looked for on all 455 sequences. None was found, for any unit.
A control for every zero: the same signature was asked of the UniProtKB entries of all mollicutes, the class of bacteria the organism was made from; each unit's note gives what came back.

Eight further signatures, of the ion channels a bacterium could have (potassium, chloride, magnesium, water and membrane-stretch channels), were looked for as well, and none was found, although each is carried by UniProtKB entries of other mollicutes.

Under extra are nine of the organism's own membrane machines that bear on what the atlas draws and match no unit. Five are named for this organism in Breuer and others 2019, whose saved text the build checks; four are listed by the signature on their sequence. All are assigned by annotation, not measured in this strain.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

method: The plant's proteins are the 27,368 of UniProt's gene-by-gene set of the reference proteome UP000006548 (release 2026_04): one for each gene, 16,212 with a reviewed entry and 11,156 with an unreviewed one.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the other species' atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.

Each signature was looked for among the InterPro entries UniProt gives each protein. A unit counts as found only where a protein carries the signature of a family that makes the machine itself; an accessory family alone does not make it found.

A plant has channels and pumps of families of its own, which no unit of the inventory stands for. They are not listed here: the search asks only for the families of Cells' units. 'Different family' is given only where the inventory's table names another family for the same machine, and it names none that a plant has.

A product with a reviewed entry is listed as a reviewed entry, one with an unreviewed entry as a family signature. Either is a candidate by family, and nothing here says which protein does which unit's work.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

species.label: Syn3A
species.plain: A bacterium with a designed, minimised genome: 452 protein-coding genes kept from Mycoplasma mycoides, in a cell about 400 nm across with one membrane and no wall. It grows on its own in a rich medium, and its genome is smaller than that of any natural cell that does.

modelled.text: JCVI-syn3A is the project's minimal-cell track (decision D173, 14 November 2026), taken up from a note that proposes it as the first whole-cell validation organism for Cells. Nothing of it is in the engine yet: the project's record holds an evidence audit, capability probes of the engine as it stands, and a proposed first milestone, with no engine code written for it and nothing accepted.

levels.label: One cell
levels.note: Drawn as a sphere 0.4 µm across with 500 ribosomes: round numbers for the smaller of the two cells that were measured. The larger one was about 0.5 µm across.

species.no_further_levels: A single-celled organism: each cell lives on its own, so there is no tissue, organ or body.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a sphere about 400 nm across; two cells measured in electron tomograms were 403 nm and 495 nm across

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: one membrane; no cell wall and no periplasm

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: no nucleus: in electron tomograms the ribosomes are spread through the whole cell, with the chromosome among them

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 543,379 base pairs

facts.label: Genes
facts.value: 493, of which 452 code for proteins; the genome record lists 455 protein products, 3 of them added for genetic manipulation

facts.label: Ribosomes
facts.value: about 500 in a small cell: 503 or 684 counted in the cell 403 nm across, by two ways of counting, and 820 or 1,095 in the one 495 nm across

facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: about 77,000 molecules in an average cell, an estimate from proteomics; 427 of the 452 kinds were detected, and the added marker tetM

facts.label: Doubling time
facts.value: about 105 minutes in rich medium

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ATP from fermenting sugar; in the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism, central metabolism is the only source of ATP

facts.label: Food
facts.value: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and cholesterol, taken up from a rich medium that is not fully defined

facts.label: Ion channels
facts.value: none found among its 455 proteins

facts.label: Division
facts.value: the division genes ftsZ and sepF are among 19 genes added to the smaller strain JCVI-syn3.0 to make this one, which gave it back a regular shape; a review reports that seven of the 19 are needed together for normal division

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: a genome designed and synthesised from that of Mycoplasma mycoides subspecies capri, strain GM12, and cut down to a minimum

cap.membrane.note: Its one membrane holds the cell's ion and proton gradients. In the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism the ATP synthase pushes protons out, against a passive leak of protons inwards; that is a model's reading, and no source read for this file measured the voltage of this strain.

cap.channels.why: No ion channel was found among its 455 proteins: none carries the signature of a channel family in Cells' catalogue, or of the bacterial channels for potassium, chloride, magnesium, water or membrane stretch, which the same search does find in other mollicutes. Its ions cross the membrane through transporters and pumps.

cap.pumps.note: Not the pumps of animal cells: it has no sodium-potassium pump. By its annotation, its ATP-driven ion movers are the ATP synthase, two P-type ATPases named as magnesium transporters, and a potassium uptake system.

cap.junctions.why: It lives as single cells and has no gap junctions: none of its proteins carries the signature of connexins or innexins.

cap.extracellular.note: Here it is the growth medium around the single cell, which the cell depends on. By the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism it takes up glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and cholesterol from a rich medium.

cap.water.note: It has no cell wall: nothing but the membrane bounds its volume.

cap.calcium.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum: it is a bacterium with a single membrane and no internal compartments, and none of its proteins carries the signature of the store's calcium pump or of its release channels.

cap.energy.note: Its ATP comes from fermenting sugar in the cytoplasm: in the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism, central metabolism is the only source of ATP.

cap.mitochondria.why: It is a bacterium and has no mitochondria. Its ATP synthase sits in the cell membrane.

cap.circuits.note: At the chromosome, which lies in the cytoplasm: there is no nucleus. The 2019 paper notes how few regulatory proteins the minimised genome has left.

cap.grn.why: It forms no tissue, so there is nothing for gene networks to be coupled across. Gene expression within the one cell belongs with regulatory circuits.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi. By its annotation, new membrane proteins are put straight into the cell membrane by the Sec translocon and the YidC insertase.

cap.machines.note: About 500 ribosomes, with RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase and the protein translocon. None of its proteins carries the proteasome's signature; its annotation lists the proteases FtsH and Lon.

cap.secretion.note: By the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism it releases the end products of sugar breakdown, lactate and acetate, into the medium and takes nutrients up. Signalling between its cells was not looked for.

cap.repair.note: The place would be its bare membrane. No source read for this file describes a membrane injury or its resealing in this organism.

cap.division.note: It grows and divides as a single cell. The division genes ftsZ and sepF are among 19 genes that were added to the smaller strain JCVI-syn3.0 to make it, which gave it back a regular shape; a review reports that seven of the 19 are needed together for normal division.

cap.replacement.why: It forms no tissue, so there is no neighbour for a new cell to replace.

cap.mechanics.why: It forms no sheet: its cells share no edges to pull on.

cap.sheet.why: It lives as single cells and forms no sheet of coupled cells.

species.label: M. pneumoniae
species.plain: A small bacterium of the human airways, among the smallest organisms that copy themselves: 688 proteins in the genome record frozen here, in a thin cell about 2 µm long with one membrane, no wall and an attachment organelle at one end.

modelled.text: Its public measurements were audited beside the minimal-cell track on JCVI-syn3A (decision D173; the track's note of 15 November 2026), which recommends it to lead a later stage on energy, transport and pH. Nothing of it is in the engine, and no model of it has run.

levels.label: One cell
levels.note: Drawn as a rod 2 µm long and 0.2 µm across, the upper ends of the ranges given for the cell, with 300 ribosomes. The real cell is not a plain rod: it changes shape, and one end narrows into the attachment organelle, about 0.3 µm long, which this shape cannot show.

species.no_further_levels: A single-celled organism: each cell lives on its own, on the cells of its host, so it has no tissue, organ or body of its own.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a thin cell 1 to 2 µm long and 0.1 to 0.2 µm wide, of changeable shape, drawn out at one end into its attachment organelle; one paper gives its volume as 0.075 µm³

facts.label: Attachment organelle
facts.value: a membrane protrusion at one pole, 250 to 300 nm long, with an internal core; it carries the adhesins and leads the cell when it glides

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: a cell membrane stiffened by sterols, and no cell wall; UniProt's curated entries of its proteins name one membrane, the cell membrane, and no outer one

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: a small prokaryote, among the smallest organisms that copy themselves: a bacterium, with no nucleus

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 816,394 base pairs

facts.label: Genes
facts.value: 688 protein products in the genome record frozen here, the re-annotation of 2000; a review counts 687 genes, a re-annotation of 2015 has 694 reading frames, and UniProt has 686 entries

facts.label: Ribosomes
facts.value: about 300 in a cell: the proteins of the ribosome were measured at a median of 300 copies in a cell, by mass spectrometry

facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: about 120,000 protein molecules in a cell, the sum over 528 kinds of protein measured by mass spectrometry, three quarters of all its kinds

facts.label: Doubling time
facts.value: about 8 hours in rich medium; 17.6 hours were measured in a serum-free medium

facts.label: Essential genes
facts.value: 342 of 694 genes essential, 93 needed for normal growth and 259 dispensable, by transposon mutagenesis

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ATP from fermenting glucose, with lactate and acetate as end products; mycoplasmas lack the citric acid cycle

facts.label: Food
facts.value: glucose as its main fuel; it makes almost none of its own building blocks, no amino acids, vitamins or lipids among them, and takes them up

facts.label: Ion channels
facts.value: none found among its 688 proteins; one glycerol facilitator of the aquaporin family

facts.label: Division
facts.value: in two, by binary fission; the attachment organelle is duplicated first and takes part in the division

facts.label: Movement
facts.value: glides on surfaces, attachment organelle first, at up to 1 µm a second

facts.label: Name
facts.value: databases now list it as Mycoplasmoides pneumoniae; the papers cited call it Mycoplasma pneumoniae

cap.membrane.note: Its one membrane holds the cell's ion and proton gradients. In a model of its metabolism published in 2020 the ATP synthase runs in reverse and pumps protons out of the cell; that is the model's result, and no source read for this file measured the voltage.

cap.channels.why: No ion channel was found among its 688 proteins: none carries the signature of a channel family in Cells' catalogue, or of the bacterial channels for potassium, chloride, magnesium or membrane stretch, which the same search does find in other mollicutes. One protein, the glycerol facilitator GlpF, carries the signature of the family of water and glycerol channels; it is not an ion channel.

cap.pumps.note: Not the pumps of animal cells: it has no sodium-potassium pump. By its annotation, its ATP-driven ion movers are the ATP synthase, one P-type ATPase whose ion is not known, and a potassium uptake system.

cap.junctions.why: It lives as single cells and has no gap junctions: none of its proteins carries the signature of connexins or innexins.

cap.extracellular.note: Here it is what surrounds the single cell: the surface of the airway cells it lives on, or a growth medium. The cell depends on it: it makes no amino acids, vitamins or lipids of its own and takes them up.

cap.water.note: It has no cell wall: nothing but the membrane bounds its volume. One of its proteins, GlpF, belongs to the family of water and glycerol channels.

cap.calcium.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum: it is a bacterium with a single membrane and no internal compartments, and none of its proteins carries the signature of the store's calcium pump or of its release channels.

cap.energy.note: Its ATP comes from fermenting sugar in the cytoplasm, with lactate and acetate as end products; mycoplasmas lack the citric acid cycle.

cap.mitochondria.why: It is a bacterium and has no mitochondria. Its ATP synthase sits in the cell membrane.

cap.circuits.note: At the chromosome, which lies in the cytoplasm: there is no nucleus.

cap.grn.why: It forms no tissue, so there is nothing for gene networks to be coupled across. Gene expression within the one cell belongs with regulatory circuits.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi. By its annotation, new membrane proteins are put straight into the cell membrane by the Sec translocon and the YidC insertase.

cap.machines.note: About 300 ribosomes, with RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase, the protein translocon and the machinery in its attachment organelle that lets it glide. None of its proteins carries the proteasome's signature; its annotation lists the proteases FtsH and Lon.

cap.secretion.note: It releases lactate and acetate, the end products of its fermentation, and takes its nutrients up. Signalling between its own cells was not looked for.

cap.repair.note: The place would be its bare membrane. No source read for this file describes a membrane injury or its resealing in this organism.

cap.division.note: It divides in two as a single cell. Its attachment organelle is duplicated first and takes part in the division; the division gene ftsZ is in its genome.

cap.replacement.why: It forms no tissue, so there is no neighbour for a new cell to replace.

cap.mechanics.why: It forms no sheet: its cells share no edges to pull on. Its own movement, gliding on a surface, is not what this capability models.

cap.sheet.why: It lives as single cells and forms no sheet of coupled cells.

species.label: E. coli
species.plain: A rod-shaped bacterium of the animal gut: 4,403 proteins in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12, in a cell a few micrometres long with two membranes and a wall between them. It swims with flagella.

modelled.text: The project's record adds it as a data-only organism, for a proposed track whose first stage is bacterial chemotaxis in a well-mixed cell; the track is on hold (decision D179, 15 November 2026). Nothing of it is in the engine: no organism definition, no model and no run.

levels.label: One cell
levels.note: Drawn as a rod 2.5 µm long and 1 µm across: the picture's choice, within the ranges given for the cell. Its second membrane and its wall are drawn as clear shells around the cell membrane, and its 6,800 ribosomes are the low end of the range one paper gives. Its flagella and fimbriae are given as appendages, with the ranges their sources give; that the fimbriae stand all over the cell is the picture's choice, since no source read for this file says where they stand.

species.no_further_levels: A single-celled organism: each cell lives on its own, so there is no tissue, organ or body.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a straight rod; earlier work put its average length between 1.6 and 3.1 µm and its width at 0.7 to 1.1 µm, and one study measured 1.6 µm (cells at rest) to 3.9 µm (cells growing on a rich medium) in length and 1.26 µm in width

facts.label: Volume
facts.value: 1.5 to 4.4 femtolitres, by the conditions it grows in

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: two membranes: the inner one separates the cytoplasm from the periplasm, the outer one the periplasm from the cell's surroundings; the cell wall lies between them

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: a bacterium, with no nucleus: its chromosome lies in a region of the cytoplasm that no membrane surrounds

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 4,641,652 base pairs

facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: 4,403 in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12, every one with a reviewed entry

facts.label: Ribosomes
facts.value: between 6,800 and 72,000 in a cell, depending on its phase of growth, as one open paper sums up earlier estimates

facts.label: Movement
facts.value: swims with flagella that grow all over its surface, or does not move

facts.label: Flagella
facts.value: 1 to 5 on a cell in one study of single cells, and 3.4 on average by another paper; each a thread typically 5 to 10 µm long (7.5 µm by one measurement). Of the width the sources disagree: about 20 nm by one, 40 nm by another

facts.label: Where the flagella stand
facts.value: all over the cell body; the motor at the foot of each sits in the inner membrane, where its ring protein FliF and its stator proteins MotA and MotB are stated to be. 34 proteins are parts of the flagellum by the Gene Ontology terms UniProt gives them

facts.label: Type 1 fimbriae
facts.value: 200 to 500 on a cell by one paper's summary, each up to 1 µm long and about 7 to 10 nm wide, standing out from the outer membrane

facts.label: Chemotaxis
facts.value: 22 of its proteins carry UniProt's keyword for chemotaxis (aer, cheA, cheB, cheR, cheW, cheY, cheZ, dppA, fliG, fliJ, fliL, fliM, fliN, fliO, mglB, motA, motB, rbsB, tap, tar, trg and tsr), and 34 are parts of the flagellum by the Gene Ontology terms UniProt gives them

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: respiration and fermentation: it lives with or without oxygen

facts.label: Where it lives
facts.value: the lower gut of animals; it survives when released to the natural environment

facts.label: Ion channels

cap.membrane.note: It has two membranes. By UniProt's vocabulary the inner one separates the cytoplasm from the periplasm, and the outer one the periplasm from the cell's surroundings. No source read for this file measured a voltage across either.

cap.channels.note: Not the channels of animal cells: none of its proteins carries the signature of a channel family that Cells has a law for. 15 of its proteins carry the signature of a bacterial channel family: the potassium channel domain (kch); the large-conductance mechanosensitive channel (MscL) (mscL); the mechanosensitive channel MscS (mscK, mscM, mscS, ybdG, ybiO and ynaI); chloride channels of the ClC family (clcA, clcB and yfeO); aquaporins and their relatives (major intrinsic proteins) (aqpZ and glpF); CorA-type magnesium channels (corA and zntB).

cap.pumps.note: Not the pumps of animal cells: none of its proteins carries the signature of the sodium-potassium pump. Its P-type ATPases (copA, kdpB, mgtA and zntA) and its ATP synthase are stated to be in the inner membrane.

cap.junctions.why: It lives as single cells and has no gap junctions: none of its proteins carries the signature of connexins or innexins.

cap.extracellular.note: Two spaces lie beyond its inner membrane: the periplasm, between its two membranes, and what surrounds the cell, the lower gut of an animal or wherever it is released.

cap.water.note: By UniProt's vocabulary a wall lies between its two membranes and plays a part in the cell's shape and stability. One of its proteins, AqpZ, carries the signature of the aquaporin family.

cap.calcium.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum, the store this capability concerns: no entry of its proteome states a place in one, and none of its proteins carries the signature of the store's calcium pump or of its release channels.

cap.energy.note: It lives by respiration and by fermentation, with or without oxygen; its ATP synthase is stated to be in the inner membrane.

cap.mitochondria.why: It is a bacterium and has no mitochondria: no entry of its proteome states a place in one. Its ATP synthase is in the inner membrane.

cap.circuits.note: At the chromosome, which lies in a region of the cytoplasm that no membrane surrounds: there is no nucleus. 64 of its proteins carry UniProt's keyword for two-component regulatory systems.

cap.grn.why: It forms no tissue, so there is nothing for gene networks to be coupled across. Gene expression within the one cell belongs with regulatory circuits.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi: no entry of its proteome states a place in either. By the names of their entries, its proteins cross or enter the inner membrane through the Sec and Tat translocases.

cap.machines.note: Its ribosomes, RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase, the protein translocases and the motor of its flagella. One of its proteins carries the signature of the proteasome's subunits: its entry names it "ATP-dependent protease subunit HslV".

cap.secretion.note: Some of its proteins are stated to be secreted, and porins and transporters carry molecules across its two membranes. Signalling between its own cells was not looked for.

cap.repair.note: The place would be its envelope. No source read for this file describes an injury of it or its resealing in this organism.

cap.division.note: It divides as a single cell: its proteome names the cell division protein FtsZ.

cap.replacement.why: It forms no tissue, so there is no neighbour for a new cell to replace.

cap.mechanics.why: It forms no sheet: its cells share no edges to pull on. Its own movement, swimming with flagella, is not what this capability models.

cap.sheet.why: It lives as single cells and forms no sheet of coupled cells.

entities.label: One identity per species
entities.plain: Each kind of molecule gets one identity and one conserved total, declared once where a world is defined, however many arrays hold it: free and bound molecules of one kind are one species. New laws then need no checks against each other's species lists, which operators make pair by pair today. Sums over species follow one declared order everywhere, so that raising the limit on the number of species later needs only a check on one test world and a cost measurement; which order is settled by one bounded comparison first (D176). A probe found that a fixed order moves results at rounding only, so it lands last in the round, alone, at a declared tolerance, and every registered protocol is run again. In development on the integration branch since 15 November 2026; not on main.

entities.label: Fuel as shared species
entities.plain: Decided on 15 November 2026 (D176): ATP, ADP and phosphate become ordinary species of the shared inventory. Reactions make and spend them, pumps draw from the same amounts, and the standard chemical potential of each is declared in one place. Fuel that is held constant is a held row of that inventory, not a parameter of a pump. The first case is small: one regeneration reaction and one pump share a finite amount of fuel, and show depletion, a slower pump and recovery, checked against an independent reference. Two boundaries are still open: how this meets explicit proton chemistry, and that work booked by a reaction is not fuel. Today finite fuel exists only in the earlier tissue families, and the tissue model holds its fuel constant. Designed; not on main.

entities.label: Passive permeation law
entities.plain: A law for molecules that cross a membrane on their own, down their gradient. In a closed test with two compartments it must conserve material, stop when both sides are at equal chemical potential, reverse with the driving force, and turn the free energy lost into heat with no work from outside. The engine's present operator for secretion and uptake is a driven route that books work, so it does not count as passive. This is the one law added in the rework round, to show that adding a law changes nothing for worlds that do not use it; its core computation already exists in the tissue model's own membrane transport. The minimal-cell track's vesicle tests are its first user. In development on the integration branch since 15 November 2026; not on main.

entities.label: Scoped composition (door S)
entities.plain: How several operators share one field. Today one operator supplies a field and replaces all of it, so two operators that touch different cells of the same field cannot be combined. In the rework each operator declares which cells or nodes it reads and changes, whether its change adds, multiplies or replaces, and at which stage of the step; the composite model then merges the changes place by place. Two operators that change separate places must give the same result in either order, and an overlap is refused unless a rule says how to combine it. Its design note was proposed on 15 November 2026. Its test case is a chain: a dose in the bath, uptake, a compartment, and a reaction inside it. In development on the integration branch since 15 November 2026; not on main.

So far it is an evidence audit, capability probes that ran the engine as it stands on a vesicle, and a first milestone designed in its note: neutral molecules and water crossing protein-free vesicles, with only numerical content judged. That milestone cannot be judged on today's engine: it starts from a trace amount, which the energy ledger refuses, and it needs the passive permeation law of the modular rework. Its numerical vesicle, pH and fuel qualifications may proceed (D176, 15 November 2026). No engine code was written for it, and nothing is accepted. The public data of a second organism, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, were audited too, and it is recommended to lead a later stage on energy, transport and pH. Authors are never contacted; missing data are looked for in public sources only, and data under non-commercial licences are used for analysis only.

entities.label: Results gate
entities.plain: How the rework is accepted. A machine-readable list names every scientific result that must still hold, and the gate fails if any of them did not actually run. planarian.note: By their signatures, planarians have innexins and no connexins. 68 planarian gene models carry the innexin signature and none the connexin one; no UniProtKB entry of any flatworm carries the connexin signature either, while 21 reviewed human entries do. One planarian innexin has a sequence record of its own, smedinx-11. More is to be read in Abascal and Zardoya 2013, on which animals have each family, and in Oviedo and Levin 2007, on that innexin; neither states an open licence, so nothing is taken from them. Which innexins a general gap-junction law would stand for is not known.

Gap junctions join the neighbouring cells of a tissue, and this organism lives as single cells.

thalecress.note: None of its 27,368 proteins carries the signature of connexins and innexins (IPR000500, IPR013092, IPR000990). The unit's human candidates carry them, so the search finds the family where it exists. A plant's cells are joined in another way: by plasmodesmata, channels lined by the cell membrane that cross the wall between two cells (UniProt's vocabulary). 32 proteins of the catalogue are stated to be there; they stand on the cell membrane's shelf.

mpneumoniae.note: None of the 688 protein products of its genome carries the signature of connexins and innexins (IPR000500, IPR013092, IPR000990). No UniProtKB entry of any mollicute, the class of bacteria it belongs to, carries them either. The unit's human candidates carry them, so the search finds the family where it exists. Gap junctions join the neighbouring cells of a tissue, and this organism lives as single cells.

planarian.note: There is no connexin 45 to find in a planarian: by its signatures it has innexins, another family of gap-junction proteins, and no connexins. 68 planarian gene models carry the innexin signature and none the connexin one; no UniProtKB entry of any flatworm carries the connexin signature either, while 21 reviewed human entries do. One planarian innexin has a sequence record of its own, smedinx-11. More is to be read in Abascal and Zardoya 2013, on which animals have each family, and in Oviedo and Levin 2007, on that innexin; neither states an open licence, so nothing is taken from them. Nothing says which innexins, if any, would form a channel like this one.

syn3a.note: None of the 455 protein products of its genome carries the signature of connexins and innexins (IPR000500, IPR013092, IPR000990). No UniProtKB entry of any mollicute, the class of bacteria it was made from, carries them either. The unit's human candidates carry them, so the search finds the family where it exists. Gap junctions join the neighbouring cells of a tissue, and this organism lives as single cells.

thalecress.note: None of its 27,368 proteins carries the signature of connexins and innexins (IPR000500, IPR013092, IPR000990). The unit's human candidates carry them, so the search finds the family where it exists. A plant's cells are joined in another way: by plasmodesmata, channels lined by the cell membrane that cross the wall between two cells (UniProt's vocabulary). 32 proteins of the catalogue are stated to be there; they stand on the cell membrane's shelf.

entities.label: Cx40/Cx37 heterotypic gap-junction channel

mpneumoniae.note: None of the 688 protein products of its genome carries the signature of connexins and innexins (IPR000500, IPR013092, IPR000990). No UniProtKB entry of any mollicute, the class of bacteria it belongs to, carries them either. The unit's human candidates carry them, so the search finds the family where it exists. Gap junctions join the neighbouring cells of a tissue, and this organism lives as single cells.

planarian.note: There is no connexin 40 or connexin 37 to find in a planarian: by its signatures it has innexins, another family of gap-junction proteins, and no connexins. 68 planarian gene models carry the innexin signature and none the connexin one; no UniProtKB entry of any flatworm carries the connexin signature either, while 21 reviewed human entries do. One planarian innexin has a sequence record of its own, smedinx-11. More is to be read in Abascal and Zardoya 2013, on which animals have each family, and in Oviedo and Levin 2007, on that innexin; neither states an open licence, so nothing is taken from them. Nothing says which innexins, if any, would form a channel like this one.

thalecress.note: None of its 27,368 proteins carries the signature of connexins and innexins (IPR000500, IPR013092, IPR000990).
